derives_from: No published Yoruba pronunciation-respelling key exists to borrow -- Yoruba lexicography prints no such column, the same absence Hausa's and Amharic's own entries record, because Standard orthography is shallow enough that a dictionary does not need one. What this table derives from instead is the same real, observable system Hausa's own table reads: the way Yoruba itself spells a foreign loanword in newspapers, signage and everyday print -- kọ́mpútà (computer), báńkì (bank), sìgá/sìgárẹ́ẹ̀tì (cigarette), fóònù (phone), rédíò (radio), pásípọ́ọ̀tù (passport). Every one collapses a consonant cluster with an inserted vowel and a foreign sound onto the nearest native letter, which is what `syllable_fixups` and the `any`-slot table below do mechanically. Adapted in shape from `ha__ha-NG.json`, the corpus's other West African CV-syllable Latin orthography, with the consonant table kept largely as Hausa measured it (both languages license no onset or coda clusters at all, so `max_onset: 1` is not a compromise for either) and the vowel table rebuilt outright: Hausa's own vowels do not distinguish close-mid from open-mid at either height, so its table collapses e/ɛ and o/ɔ onto one letter apiece, where Yoruba's alphabet carries that exact distinction as `e`/`ẹ` and `o`/`ọ` -- collapsing it here would throw away the one thing this reader's own script is built to keep.

deviations.why: Yoruba has no voiced non-labial fricative at all -- the native inventory is b d dʒ ɡ for voiced obstruents and f s ʃ h for voiceless fricatives, with nothing voiced among the fricatives -- so /z/ is folded to its voiceless counterpart `s`, the same voicing-neutralising move this table already makes for /v/->`f`.

deviations.for: tʃ and its affricate relatives (ʈʂʰ, tɕʰ, tʃʲ, tɕ, ʈʂ)
deviations.why: Yoruba has no <c> letter and no voiceless affricate of its own -- only the voiced dʒ, spelt `j`. Hausa's table reads these onto `c`, which is Hausa's own letter for exactly this affricate; Yoruba has no equivalent, so the class is read onto `ṣ`, the fricative Yoruba does have at the same place of articulation, rather than onto `j`, which would misrepresent voicing in the direction a reader is more likely to notice.

Kept as its own letter in Hausa's own table, because Hausa has an implosive series and a native letter for it. Yoruba has neither, so the plain stop `d` is the nearest sound rather than a borrowed letter this reader's own alphabet does not contain.

approximations.why: Boko has no th/dh digraph and Hausa has neither sound natively. s is the closest voiceless fricative at the same place a Hausa mouth reaches for; d is the closest the voiced counterpart has, matching how Hausa's own borrowings from English routinely substitute a plain stop or fricative for th (as fasfo does for the English /s/ cluster in passport, folding a whole consonant sequence onto the nearest Hausa shape).

Hausa has no phonemic /v/; loanwords from English and French regularly fold it to f, the voiceless counterpart at the same place, the same substitution es/it/de readers make for sounds just outside their own inventory.

approximations.sounds: /ə ɜ ɚ ɝ ʌ/ (English about, bird, water, cup)
approximations.why: Hausa has no reduced central vowel and does not weaken unstressed vowels the way English does, so an unstressed English syllable is read at full value whatever is written. a is the closest of Hausa's five vowels to schwa's mid-central quality, the same choice Swahili's and Malay's own tables make for the identical reason.

approximations.sounds: /y ø œ ɯ ʉ ʏ/ (front rounded and back unrounded vowels)
approximations.out: u u e e u u
approximations.why: Hausa's five vowels are all unrounded-front or rounded-back in the ordinary way; a front rounded vowel is read as its nearest back-rounded cousin (u) and a back unrounded vowel the same way, except the two mid-front rounded vowels ø/œ, which read closer to e.

policy_note:
max_onset: 1, and not a compromise -- Yoruba syllable structure is strictly (C)V, with no onset or coda consonant clusters anywhere in the native vocabulary, so `reader_onsets` is omitted the same way Mandarin's own table omits it: the field would be read at max_onset 1 and do nothing. Every consonant cluster a foreign word's IPA presents is therefore broken across syllables by `syllabify` alone, which is the mechanical version of what Yoruba's own loanword spelling already does by ear (sukulu for school, búrẹ́dì for bread -- a vowel inserted to open every cluster). 

stress: caps, not none, for the same reason `ha`'s own table gives: Yoruba itself has no contrastive stress, so this device never fires on a Yoruba word, but marking a foreign word's stressed syllable is still a real signal to a reader approximating an unfamiliar pronunciation, and capitalisation does not collide with anything Yoruba's own orthography uses the letter case for. 

tone: drop, matching Punjabi's own reader table rather than the three that keep it -- Punjabi is itself a tone language and still chose drop for its own reader, on the grounds that a respelling is approximating a foreign word's segments, not composing a second, independently-tuned tone melody on top of them. The same argument applies here with more force: Yoruba's tone is register, not contour, so folding an arbitrary foreign pitch contour onto three Yoruba tone levels would assert a specific tone melody with no real source in the word being read, on every single respelling in every one of Yoruba's 42 target pairs -- a much larger and less defensible claim than the one Vietnamese, Thai and Mandarin's own readers make about each other's genuinely cognate tone systems. 

length: none. Yoruba writes a long vowel by doubling only in a dictionary headword, the same convention `ha_to_ipa`'s own note records for Hausa, and this pack's own `text` column does not use it, so there is no established reading convention for a reader to lean on here either.
legend: Kò sí àmì tuntun -- gbogbo lẹ́tà jẹ́ ti Yorùbá ní ìbámu. LẸ́TÀ ÀGBÀ = ìdí tí ó ní agbára (níbi tí èdè ìpìlẹ̀ ti ní irú u rẹ̀).
note: What this reads for and what it does not. Yoruba's own tone is fully spelt in `data/lang/yo`'s own `text` column, which is the thing this file does not touch -- this table is the mirror direction, spelling *other* languages' IPA in Yoruba letters for a Yoruba reader, and `policy.tone: drop` means a foreign tone contour is never asserted here (see `policy_note`). What it keeps that Hausa's sibling table does not: the close-mid/open-mid vowel distinction Yoruba's own alphabet already marks (e/ẹ, o/ọ), rebuilt from measurement rather than carried over blind -- see `derives_from`. Nasal vowels are spelt with the subdotted letter for the front and back open-mid categories (ẹn, ọn) rather than the plain-letter `en`/`on` Hausa's own table would use for the identical IPA, because standard Yoruba orthography never writes `en` or `on` as a nasal vowel -- only `ẹn`/`ọn` are legal nasal spellings, so `en`/`on` would misparse as a plain vowel followed by an onset `n` rather than read as nasal at all. Checked with `node scripts/respell_check.mjs yo --gaps` before being trusted, not assumed.
